data.name: Costa Rica
data.summary: Costa Rica taxes individuals only on Costa Rican-source income, so a foreign portfolio's dividends and gains are not taxed locally. Local capital gains and dividends are taxed at 15%. There is no inheritance, gift or net wealth tax; property tax is 0.25% plus a luxury home tax on expensive homes. Foreign passive income held through a Costa Rican company in a multinational group can be taxed.

regimes.name: Ordinary tax residence (territorial)
regimes.description: Individuals are taxed only on Costa Rican-source income. Foreign dividends, interest and gains are not taxed for individuals. Costa Rican-source capital gains and dividends 15%.
regimes.eligibility: Permanent residents and individuals present six months or more in a tax year are resident.

capital_gains.summary: Costa Rican-source capital gains are taxed at 15% (Law 7092 as amended by Law 9635), with an option of 2.25% of the sale price on the first sale of an asset under certain conditions. Foreign-source gains of individuals are outside the territorial scope.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Real estate transfer tax 1.5% (PwC). Gains realised habitually in a business are taxed at ordinary rates up to 25%/30%.

capital_gains.rate_basis: 15% capital gains rate (Deloitte 2026; PwC reviewed 30 Jun 2026). Foreign gains 0 under the territorial principle (PwC: Costa Rica-source income = assets used, goods located, services rendered in Costa Rica).
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Not taxed for individuals. For companies in multinational groups, foreign passive income can be taxed (non-qualified entity rule) - relevant if the portfolio is held through a Costa Rican company.

dividends.summary: Dividends from Costa Rican companies: 15% final withholding. Foreign dividends of individuals are not taxed.

income.name: Costa Rica

income_tax.summary: Territorial tax on Costa Rican-source income. Employment income is taxed monthly at 0% to CRC 918,000, then 10%, 15%, 20% and 25% above CRC 4,727,000 a month; self-employed income uses a separate annual scale starting above CRC 6,244,000. Employees pay about 10.84% to the CCSS and others.
income_tax.self_employed_notes: Self-employed income (lucrative activities, annual net income): 0% to CRC 6,244,000; 10% to 8,329,000; 15% to 10,414,000; 20% to 20,872,000; 25% above (Deloitte 2026, Alegra). Social security for the self-employed ranges from 10.5% to 18.5% (Deloitte); 18.5% is shown as the upper bound for a USD 60,000 earner, but which tier applies depends on declared income and was not verified. Deductible expenses apply as for companies. PwC's employee share table (2026 to 2028) differs from Deloitte's 10.84%: PwC gives the worker share of the IVM pension as 4.33% from 2026 (CCSS health and Banco Popular come on top).
income_tax.local_tax_note: Brackets are the 2026 monthly employment scale (CRC 918,000 / 1,347,000 / 2,364,000 / 4,727,000, Decree 45333-H) multiplied by 12; tax on salary is withheld by the employer and there are small credits for spouse and children. Territorial: only Costa Rican-source income is taxed, no foreign tax relief. Employee contribution of 10.84% is Deloitte's figure for all employee deductions; PwC lists the IVM pension share separately (4.33% from 2026). No cap on contributions was found. No municipal income tax. PwC defines Costa Rican-source income as income derived from assets used, goods located or services rendered within Costa Rican territory, so pay for work done while living in Costa Rica is local-source income.

regimes.name: Law 10008 international remote worker and service provider visa
regimes.description: Stay of up to one year, renewable once, for remote workers and service providers earning abroad. Income from abroad is exempt from Costa Rican income tax and the holder is not treated as tax resident; the exemption does not extend to family members.
regimes.duration_note: USD 3,000 a month averaged over the last year for one person (USD 48,000 a year for a household of USD 4,000 a month, spouse income may be pooled). Renewal for a further year requires at least 180 days spent in Costa Rica in the first year. Health insurance with USD 50,000 minimum cover in Costa Rica is required.

income.residence_routes: Remote workers of any citizenship can use the Law 10008 visa (USD 3,000 a month, up to one year renewable once, USD 50,000 health cover). Employees of a Costa Rican employer need a work permit or residence (not researched here). The earlier repo research (data/jurisdictions/CRI.json) lists income- and investment-based residence categories (rentista, inversionista, pensionado) without verified thresholds. EU, US and other citizens use the same routes. US citizens remain taxable in the US on worldwide income; Costa Rican tax on Costa Rican-source income can be credited only where the US foreign tax credit rules allow.

succession.name: Costa Rica
succession.summary: Costa Rica has freedom of testation. A will must, however, secure maintenance (alimentos) for young or disabled children, the spouse and parents who need it (Civil Code art. 595); the legítima of the pre-1888 code no longer exists. Trusts exist by statute (fideicomiso), foundations are non-profit, and Costa Rica is not in the Hague Trusts Convention.
succession.family_claims: The testator must secure maintenance for children until adulthood (for life if disabled), and for parents and a spouse while they need it (Código Civil art. 595); if the will does not, heirs take only what is left after that maintenance. Family Code (Ley 5476) gives the surviving spouse further rights.
succession.foreign_law_note: Not sourced. No Costa Rican conflict rule for succession and no choice of law was found.
succession.trust_note: The fideicomiso is regulated in the Código de Comercio (arts. 633 ff.), which I did not read here; common-law trusts are not part of the law and foreign trusts' treatment was not sourced. Foundations: Ley de Fundaciones (Ley 5338 of 1973) allows foundations for non-profit purposes; whether a family foundation is possible was not verified. Not in the Hague Trusts Convention.
open_questions: Code of Commerce trust articles and Ley 5338 (foundations) were not read; both entries are 'limited' pending checks.
Whether art. 595 should be read as a compulsory share is debated in the literature (see source); treated here as a maintenance duty.
Conflict rule for succession and treatment of foreign heirs were not sourced.

immigration.name: Costa Rica
immigration.summary: Costa Rica grants renewable two-year residence for investment (USD 150,000), passive income (rentista, USD 2,500 a month) or a pension (USD 1,000 a month), with permanent residence after three years. A separate non-residency digital nomad visa needs USD 3,000 a month. All groups (EU, US, other) use the same routes.
immigration.naturalisation: Seven years of legal residence, or five for nationals of Central American and Ibero-American countries and Spain; language and history tests (details not read officially).
immigration.dual_citizenship_note: Costa Rica does not require renunciation of another nationality (general position; not source-checked in this session).

routes.name: Inversionista (investor) residence
routes.summary: Two-year renewable residence for investing at least USD 150,000 (USD 100,000 for forestry) in Costa Rica; permanent residence after 3 years.
routes.requirements: Investment of at least USD 150,000 (lowered from USD 200,000 by Law 9996), or USD 100,000 for qualifying forestry; real estate must be held in the applicant's own name. Temporary residence is 2 years, renewable; permanent residence is available after 3 years of temporary residence. Contributions to the social security fund (CCSS) are required. Migration Law 8764.
routes.fees_note: Filing and change-of-status fees are indicatively USD 250 to 500 in total per one guide; not read from the migration authority.
routes.physical_presence: Not stated in the sources reviewed; see open questions
routes.processing_time: Longer than 9 to 12 months for inversionista (guide)
routes.tax_note: Costa Rica taxes territorially; residence is not automatically tax residence.

routes.name: Rentista residence
routes.summary: Two-year renewable residence for people with USD 2,500 a month of non-work income for two years, or a USD 60,000 deposit.
routes.requirements: USD 2,500 a month (USD 30,000 a year) of non-employment income certified for 24 months, or a USD 60,000 deposit in an approved Costa Rican bank that pays out the monthly amount; the income must be exchanged through the Costa Rican banking system.

routes.summary: Two-year renewable residence for retirees with a lifetime pension of at least USD 1,000 a month.
routes.requirements: Lifetime pension of at least USD 1,000 a month (USD 12,000 a year); a married couple can qualify on one pension; USD 1,000 a month must be exchanged through the Costa Rican banking system; one guide says only pensions count, not rental or dividends.

routes.name: Digital nomad visa (Law 10008)
routes.summary: A one-year stay, renewable once, for remote workers earning USD 3,000 a month (USD 4,000 for a family). It is not a residency category.
routes.requirements: Income of USD 3,000 a month (USD 36,000 a year), or USD 4,000 for a family, from foreign sources; health insurance of at least USD 50,000 for the whole stay; bank statements for 12 months. Initial one year, renewable once. Time does not count towards residency. The tourism board's landing page reportedly lists USD 5,000 for families; the law and regulation say USD 4,000.
routes.physical_presence: Up to one year per grant, renewable once
routes.tax_note: Foreign earnings of visa holders are not taxed in Costa Rica; US citizens stay taxable in the US.
